label: I
title: Introduction to ML Systems
description: Data, algorithms, and machines on a single system.

concepts.label: Dual mandate
concepts.claim: Every ML system must show both that its learned behavior is trustworthy and that the machine delivers it within time, memory, energy, and cost budgets, so an accurate but slow model and a fast model trained on unrepresentative data are both failures.

concepts.label: Data defines behavior
concepts.claim: Training data plus the optimization procedure produce the program, so changing the dataset changes system behavior as surely as changing source code, and debugging, versioning, and review must extend to the data.

concepts.label: D·A·M diagnosis
concepts.claim: Attributing a symptom to Data, Algorithm, or Machine chooses the evidence and the class of fix, and relieving the binding constraint moves the bottleneck across the triad, so diagnosis is a loop of diagnose, intervene, and re-measure.

concepts.label: Iron law of ML systems
concepts.claim: Across Data, Algorithm, and Machine, execution time factors as samples per task times FLOPs per sample times seconds per FLOP (where the first two multiply to total operations O), and unpacks on hardware into bytes moved over bandwidth plus operations over peak rate times utilization plus fixed overhead, with ideal overlap giving the larger of the first two plus overhead, so a faster component helps only through the share of time it changes.

concepts.label: Three efficiency levers
concepts.claim: Data selection cuts samples per task, algorithmic efficiency lowers FLOPs per sample, and compute efficiency lowers realized seconds per FLOP by raising utilization and reducing stalls, while return on compute (accuracy gained per added cost) tests whether an added investment is worth its price.

concepts.label: Silent degradation
concepts.claim: ML adds a failure route in which code, runtime, and health checks stay green while predictive quality falls as the operating population shifts or training and serving transforms diverge, and locally accuracy falls by a fitted sensitivity times the divergence (eq-degradation), where divergence prompts investigation and labeled outcomes establish loss.

concepts.label: Bitter lesson and bottleneck migration
concepts.claim: General methods that turn computation into capability have repeatedly overtaken encoded human knowledge, so each AI era traded one binding limit for the next and today's limit is the infrastructure: memory, bandwidth, power, and orchestration.

concepts.label: The system is the model
concepts.claim: User-visible behavior is produced by the data pipeline, weights, execution stack, serving path, and monitoring loop together, so most of the engineering burden and the costliest failures sit outside the learned parameters, at interfaces no component test exercises.

concepts.label: Silicon contract
concepts.claim: Each tier's hardware offers a peak compute rate, a memory bandwidth, and a fixed overhead that enter the iron law's three terms, while memory capacity and energy act as feasibility preconditions that can rule a tier out before any term is evaluated.

concepts.label: Workload archetypes and lighthouses
concepts.claim: Classifying a workload by what binds it first gives four archetypes, compute-bound (ResNet-50 training), bandwidth-bound (batch-one LLM decode), capacity-bound (DLRM embeddings), and power-bound (keyword spotting), and the class is a regime, not a model property, since batch, precision, or hardware can move a model across it.

concepts.label: Physical walls set deployment tiers
concepts.claim: The light barrier puts a round-trip floor under any remote path, the power wall (dynamic power roughly cubic in frequency) caps sustained mobile power at a few watts, and the memory wall makes data movement a growing share of time, so cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML are constraint regimes spanning about nine orders of magnitude in power and memory.

concepts.label: Device energy budgets
concepts.claim: On untethered devices energy per inference is first-order with two distinct limits, a battery budget fixable by duty cycling or a lighter model and a thermal ceiling on sustained power that throttles regardless of charge, and transmitting raw data can cost more energy than inferring locally.

concepts.label: Data locality invariant
concepts.claim: A remote path is rejected when even its lower bound (transfer time plus propagation plus remote compute) exceeds the deadline, because transmission and propagation cannot be bought down with more remote compute, and only surviving paths are compared on measured time.

concepts.label: Screen then cost
concepts.claim: Choosing where to run applies successive filters, first whether ML beats a simpler baseline (the complexity tax), then privacy, latency, resource, and cost gates, comparing cost only among survivors on matched lifecycle budgets, and an empty set forces redesign or partitioning.

concepts.label: Hybrid partitioning
concepts.claim: When no single tier satisfies a whole pipeline, stages go where their binding term is cheapest through train-serve splits, hierarchical filtering and confidence cascades, and progressive deployment, at the price of keeping features, versions, and preprocessing synchronized across tiers.

concepts.label: Memory wall
concepts.claim: Compute has grown faster than memory bandwidth (about 1.6x versus 1.2x per year), so data movement takes an ever larger share of time and energy at every tier.

concepts.label: Bottleneck principle
concepts.claim: In a pipelined system throughput is set by the slowest stage and overlapped stages cost the maximum of their times, so effort on any stage but the binding one buys nothing.

concepts.label: Data gravity
concepts.claim: Shipping data over a network grows with data volume while shipping the computation does not, so large datasets pull computation to where the data lives.

concepts.label: Total cost of ownership
concepts.claim: Comparing deployment paradigms needs the total cost of ownership, the upfront capital plus recurring operating expense (power, cooling, egress, storage, labor) over the system's lifetime, because hourly accelerator rates hide most of the bill and low utilization makes fixed pools expensive.

concepts.label: The lifecycle is a loop
concepts.claim: An ML system moves through problem definition, data, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring, each handing the next a concrete artifact, and because learned behavior changes when the world changes, monitoring evidence must flow back to earlier stages, so deployment starts an operational phase rather than ending the project.

concepts.label: Constraint propagation
concepts.claim: A constraint discovered late forces rework in every upstream artifact that relied on its absence (the 4 GB model against a 500 MB device reservation), so rework is estimated by tracing the revise, retrain, and revalidate chain, and propagation runs both backward and forward.

concepts.label: Problem framing
concepts.claim: A request becomes a requirement only when stated as a measurable improvement over a named baseline and decomposed into statistical, physical, and operational constraints bound before development, because a metric that diverges from the goal defeats the system before training starts.

concepts.label: Stage interface contracts
concepts.claim: Each stage has an input contract, an output contract, and a quality invariant, and enforcing them at the boundaries turns the feedback loop into an audit that names which upstream stage owns a defect.

concepts.label: Validation as a release gate
concepts.claim: Evaluation measures and validation decides: a release needs evidence on latency, subgroup performance, calibration, robustness across sites and time, and operational readiness, recorded in an immutable manifest, and a failed threshold routes the fix to the stage that owns it.

concepts.label: Iteration tax
concepts.claim: Cycle time bounds how many hypotheses a team can test in a fixed calendar, so iteration velocity buys search breadth rather than guaranteed accuracy, and late discoveries multiply the tax.

concepts.label: Lab-to-field gap
concepts.claim: Accuracy on a curated test set is not deployment readiness, because field captures differ from curated research images (the Thai screening deployment's ungradable images), so validation must sample the conditions the system will meet.

concepts.label: Data as code practice
concepts.claim: Because the pipeline that produces a dataset is the system's build and every retraining a rebuild, datasets need the disciplines code has: immutable lineage, executable validation suites, versioned releases, and debugging by controlled comparison of versions.

concepts.label: Data cascades
concepts.claim: A data defect entered early passes schemas and tests, is converted by each later stage into new derived state, and surfaces only at evaluation or deployment, so remediation cost scales with the downstream artifacts that consumed it and prevention belongs at the source.

concepts.label: Labels are the specification
concepts.claim: Ground truth is the system's specification, so a labeling error becomes part of the definition of correct; labeling usually dominates data cost, granularity sets per-label cost, and label quality is bounded through chance-corrected agreement, gold checks, and monitoring of agreement over time.

concepts.label: Training-serving consistency
concepts.claim: Shared feature code is not enough: fitted state (normalization constants, vocabularies, gain handling) must be fitted once on the training split, persisted with the model, and replayed identically at serving, because a skewed feature is still a valid vector and raises no error; a violation is training-serving skew, an internal divergence of logic or state that differs from drift in the environment.

concepts.label: Data leakage
concepts.claim: Train, validation, and test sets are trust boundaries, and leakage occurs when information crosses them through duplicates, split groups, future-derived features, or preprocessing fitted before the split, so splits are group-keyed, transforms are fit on train only, and features use point-in-time retrieval.

concepts.label: The feeding problem
concepts.claim: Training throughput is the minimum of the compute-limited rate and the data supply rate, and storage bandwidth, host decode, and bytes per sample each impose a slowest-stage bound, so the input path is sized for the rate the accelerator consumes.

concepts.label: Drift statistics
concepts.claim: Drift decomposes into covariate, label, and concept shift (the last detectable only with labels), and PSI, KL divergence, and the two-sample K-S statistic flag divergence as a prompt for investigation and outcome evidence, not proof of degradation.

concepts.label: Data budget from targets
concepts.claim: A product target becomes a data requirement by arithmetic: a false-wake budget fixes a per-window false-positive rate, a budget at a per-label cost buys a computed label count, and the rule of three sets the representative hours needed to support a zero-event claim.

concepts.label: Validation at the ingestion boundary
concepts.claim: The ingestion boundary admits only well-formed, plausible data through synchronous schema and contract checks plus asynchronous statistical checks, and dead-letter queues, backoff, circuit breakers, and validated fallbacks make the pipeline degrade gracefully rather than silently.

concepts.label: Dataset releases and lineage
concepts.claim: A dataset release is an immutable, versioned record of sources, split assignment, label and rubric version, and feature configuration, and data lineage links each dataset, feature, and model to what produced it, so a regression is traced by snapshot comparison instead of guesswork.

concepts.label: Storage tiers and access patterns
concepts.claim: No medium is both cheap and fast, and training's sequential scans and serving's point lookups pull in opposite directions, so ML systems match warehouses, lakes, object stores, and caches to each lifecycle phase's access pattern.

concepts.label: Data debt
concepts.claim: Data debt is the accumulated cost of implicit coupling and missing documentation across documentation, schema, quality, and freshness, measured against thresholds and paid down deliberately rather than carried unconsciously.

concepts.label: Ingestion and transformation patterns
concepts.claim: Batch versus streaming is priced by how fast data loses value, and ETL versus ELT by where the transformation boundary sits relative to storage, with loader-side transforms extending ELT into the training loop.

concepts.label: Feature stores
concepts.claim: A feature store registers each feature definition once and serves it from an offline store for training and an online store for serving, with point-in-time (as-of) retrieval so training sees only feature values available at each observation's timestamp; shared definitions reduce skew only when fitted state, timestamps, and freshness are also synchronized.

concepts.label: Network as linear maps and nonlinearities
concepts.claim: A layer is one matrix product plus bias followed by an element-wise activation and a network is their composition, without the nonlinearity the stack collapses to one linear map, and inference runs only the forward pass while training adds loss, backward pass, and update.

concepts.label: Cost from layer shapes
concepts.claim: Layer widths fix parameters, forward work (one multiply-accumulate, two FLOPs, per weight per example), and retained activations before any code runs, so width costs quadratically, depth costs linearly but adds sequential steps and saved activations.

concepts.label: Backprop over saved activations
concepts.claim: Backpropagation applies the chain rule layer by layer in reverse, each dense layer needs two backward products of forward size, so a training step costs about three times the forward matrix work and every forward activation must stay live, or be recomputed, until the backward pass reaches its layer.

concepts.label: Training holds four kinds of state
concepts.claim: Training memory is weights plus gradients plus optimizer state plus saved activations, while inference keeps only the weights and the largest adjacent pair of activation buffers, and raising the batch leaves parameter state fixed while multiplying saved activations.

concepts.label: Batching raises dense-layer intensity
concepts.claim: A dense layer is a matrix-vector product at batch one and a matrix-matrix product when batched, so batching reuses each weight across examples and raises arithmetic intensity (about 0.5 to 12 FLOP/byte from batch 1 to 32 for the running network), which can still sit on the bandwidth slope.

concepts.label: Activation functions
concepts.claim: Sigmoid and tanh saturate and need an exponential datapath, ReLU passes gradient one on its positive branch at the cost of a comparator and can die, and softmax normalizes output scores.

concepts.label: Loss and mini-batch descent
concepts.claim: Cross-entropy against a one-hot label reduces to the negative log of the correct-class probability, its fused softmax gradient is p minus y, and mini-batch gradient descent averages per-example gradients so the batch size becomes the main systems knob.

concepts.label: Numerical range
concepts.claim: A branch-free program fails by range rather than logic: saturating derivatives and initialization scale compound into vanishing or exploding gradients, small gradients flush below a format's smallest normal, and overflow propagates Inf and NaN, so the number format is part of the training contract.

concepts.label: Reject-option thresholds
concepts.claim: A classifier's scores become operational decisions only through a confidence threshold that routes uncertain inputs to review, chosen on a risk-coverage curve by an expected-cost rule over review and error costs.

concepts.label: Overfitting and regularization
concepts.claim: Overfitting shows as training loss that keeps falling while validation performance stalls or worsens, and regularization controls it at small systems cost, since weight penalties need no persistent state, dropout costs a fresh random mask per activation only during training, and early stopping relies on periodic validation and checkpoints.

concepts.label: Inductive bias buys data and cost
concepts.claim: Each architecture is defined by a structural assumption fixed before training (locality and weight sharing, ordered recurrence, content-based routing), and a bias that matches the data cuts parameters, samples, and operations while weak priors pay off only at large data and compute.

concepts.label: Every family lowers onto GEMM
concepts.claim: Convolution reaches matrix multiply through im2col or implicit GEMM, attention and LSTM gates fuse their projections into wide GEMMs, and pointwise convolutions and recommender MLPs are GEMMs, so GEMM dominates nearly every workload's operation count and the exceptions are the memory-bound remainder.

concepts.label: Architectures as cost signatures
concepts.claim: Counting weights, multiply-accumulates, and resident bytes per building block predicts which iron-law term binds: dense layers stream each weight once per batch, convolutions reuse each filter at every position, recurrence adds a serial floor, attention adds quadratic score work, and embedding lookups are copies.

concepts.label: Quadratic attention
concepts.claim: Dense self-attention computes sequence-length-squared score interactions, so doubling context quadruples that work, while materializing the score matrix is optional storage that tiled kernels remove, and attention arithmetic dominates a block only past a context of about six times the hidden size.

concepts.label: Autoregressive decode and the KV cache
concepts.claim: Prefill runs the whole prompt as weight-reusing GEMMs and is usually compute-bound, while decode emits one token per step at about 1 FLOP/byte, re-reading every weight plus a KV cache that grows linearly per token per request, so small-batch decode is bandwidth-bound.

concepts.label: Embedding capacity wall
concepts.claim: Embedding lookups map high-cardinality IDs to learned rows read at data-dependent addresses, so a recommender is capacity-first: table size decides where tables live (shrink, move, or partition) and which bandwidth the data term pays before arithmetic matters.

concepts.label: Architecture selection by workload profile
concepts.claim: The same accelerator is compute-, bandwidth-, or capacity-bound by architecture alone, so selection maps data symmetries to an operator family, filters candidates against storage, activation peak, intensity, latency, and power budgets, then validates on the target device.

concepts.label: Skip connections and normalization
concepts.claim: Residual connections keep gradients alive through deep stacks and normalization steadies forward scale, but the skip input stays live through the branch, residual adds and normalization are bandwidth-bound and want fusion, and BatchNorm adds batch dependence and training-serving skew.

concepts.label: Efficient architecture families
concepts.claim: Factoring a convolution into depthwise and pointwise stages cuts parameters and multiply-accumulates by about 8-9x for 3x3 filters, but the factored layers have low arithmetic intensity, so far fewer FLOPs need not mean proportionally faster execution.

concepts.label: Three framework problems
concepts.claim: Every framework must solve execution, differentiation, and hardware abstraction; the model fixes the operation count while the framework shapes the other iron-law terms, with execution bearing on overhead, differentiation on bytes, and abstraction on efficiency.

concepts.label: Eager, graph, and JIT execution
concepts.claim: Eager execution exposes intermediate values to ordinary debugging but shows the runtime one operation at a time, static graphs give the compiler whole-program visibility at the price of graph-only control flow, and graph-capture JIT guards captured regions and pays a graph break wherever capture fails.

concepts.label: Dispatch overhead law
concepts.claim: Each eagerly dispatched operation pays a fixed host cost of microseconds, so a workload of many small kernels is overhead-bound when total dispatch time exceeds device time, while large GEMM-dominated layers are device-bound; compilation, fusion, larger batches, and graph replay are the levers.

concepts.label: Kernel fusion
concepts.claim: Most elementwise and normalization operators are memory-bound, so fusing a chain of k of them into one kernel cuts idealized traffic from 2kNb to 2Nb and removes k-1 launches, but a compiler fuses only what it sees together and fusion cannot drop values a backward rule must read.

concepts.label: Reverse-mode autodiff
concepts.claim: Reverse mode propagates adjoints as vector-Jacobian products from a scalar loss and yields every gradient in one backward sweep at a small constant multiple of forward cost, never materializing a Jacobian, at the price of a recorded graph and retained forward values.

concepts.label: Saved forward state
concepts.claim: Every backward rule reads values from the forward operating point, so saved activations grow linearly with batch and depth, peak at the start of backward, and can exceed the weights by orders of magnitude, while the recorded graph decides when each is freed and recomputation or detachment changes what is kept.

concepts.label: Compilation breakeven
concepts.claim: Compiling pays only when production executions amortize compile time, with breakeven at compile time divided by the per-run saving, so prototyping loops stay eager and long training or serving runs compile.

concepts.label: Tensor metadata and placement
concepts.claim: A tensor's shape, dtype, strides, and device select the kernel and forbid silent cross-device mixing, and because the host link runs far below device memory bandwidth, placement, pinned memory, and stream overlap decide whether transfers sit on the critical path.

concepts.label: Framework abstraction ladder
concepts.claim: Frameworks accreted bottom-up from BLAS kernels through array libraries and autodiff frameworks to graph compilers, each layer automating what the one below left to the programmer and hiding shape, dtype, device, and unit assumptions that must be checked at boundaries.

concepts.label: Module abstraction
concepts.claim: A module tree provides automatic parameter discovery, a train/eval mode flag propagated from the root, and hierarchical serialization through dotted state-dict keys, so one object can be optimized, saved, frozen, and inspected.

concepts.label: Major frameworks compared
concepts.claim: TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX each solve all three framework problems but emphasize different paths, so the useful comparison is what each lets the compiler see and which constraint to profile, not a speed leaderboard.

concepts.label: Choosing a framework
concepts.claim: A development framework is chosen by first eliminating paths that cannot export every required operator to a runtime that fits the deployment target, then ranking survivors by team pipeline and migration cost.

concepts.label: Mixed precision and checkpointing mechanics
concepts.claim: Frameworks implement mixed precision as a dispatch policy (autocast's per-operator precision list plus a gradient scaler) and activation checkpointing as recorded segments recomputed during backward, which is the machinery a training run configures.

concepts.label: Training-time law
concepts.claim: In the macroscopic D·A·M product form of the iron law, training work is about 6PD FLOPs (D tokens times 6P FLOPs per token) and run time is that work over peak rate times utilization, so every point of utilization recovered at constant power removes time, energy, and dollars in the same proportion, while memory sits outside the law as a feasibility gate.

concepts.label: Model FLOPs utilization
concepts.claim: MFU is useful model FLOPs per step over peak times measured step time and is the honest estimate of utilization, whereas the busy time a device monitor reports is only an upper bound, high for a memory-stalled job and low for a data-starved one.

concepts.label: Training memory at scale
concepts.claim: Mixed-precision Adam holds 16 bytes per parameter of static state (eight times the FP16 inference weights) before any activation, and only the activation term grows with batch and sequence length, which is what pushes a large model past one accelerator's memory.

concepts.label: Mixed precision
concepts.claim: Running eligible matrix products in FP16 or BF16 raises the attainable peak and halves activation bytes but leaves the 16 B/param static state unchanged, FP16 needs dynamic loss scaling to keep gradients above its normal floor while BF16 usually does not, and the speedup is bounded by the work that stays off the matrix units.

concepts.label: Checkpointing and accumulation
concepts.claim: Activation checkpointing recomputes segment interiors to cut activation memory from O(L) to O(sqrt L) for about one extra forward pass, and gradient accumulation builds a large effective batch from micro-batches that fit, reproducing the large-batch gradient only when losses are normalized consistently.

concepts.label: Profile to find the binding term
concepts.claim: Which technique helps depends on which resource is saturated, so the workflow is timeline first, then hardware counters, then one targeted fix and a re-profile, feasibility comes before speed, and a fix on a non-binding stage buys nothing.

concepts.label: Fine-tuning scope
concepts.claim: Training scope decides which memory terms exist: full fine-tuning of an 8B model needs about 128 GB of static state, while adapters such as LoRA shrink gradients and optimizer state to well under one percent of parameters, and activations still follow the backward path through every frozen layer.

concepts.label: Training input pipeline
concepts.claim: Training throughput is the minimum of host preparation rate, host-link rate, and compute rate, and overlap makes the step cost the maximum of the stage times but cannot raise the slowest stage, so workers, prefetch depth, and pinned memory are sized against measured demand.

concepts.label: IO-aware attention
concepts.claim: FlashAttention computes exact attention tile by tile in on-chip memory with online-softmax statistics and recomputes tiles in backward, dropping stored attention state from quadratic to linear in sequence length and cutting memory traffic without changing model FLOPs.

concepts.label: Single-node data parallelism
concepts.claim: Data parallelism replicates the model and averages gradients with AllReduce, whose per-device traffic depends on parameter count rather than batch, so splitting a fixed batch across one node's accelerators raises the share of unhidden synchronization unless it overlaps with backward.

concepts.label: Sharding within one node
concepts.claim: When per-replica state does not fit, ZeRO stages shard optimizer state, then gradients, then parameters across one node's accelerators, trading memory for communication, and layerwise model parallelism pays a pipeline bubble unless micro-batches are pipelined.

concepts.label: Training checkpoints
concepts.claim: A training checkpoint saves persistent state (weights, master copy, optimizer moments) plus scheduler, RNG, data position, and scaler state for exact resume, and checkpoint cadence trades save stalls against replayed work, so fault tolerance is a throughput decision.

concepts.label: Selection inequality
concepts.claim: A training-time claim for data selection holds only if selection time plus subset training time is less than full training time at matched quality and coverage, so scorer size and refresh rate, not the retained fraction, decide whether selection is a net saving.

concepts.label: Measuring data value
concepts.claim: Sample value is learning per unit of training compute (the information-compute ratio), learning-curve metrics show whether a reduction held quality, and a gain in data value becomes a throughput gain only when the run is compute-bound and the saved work is on the critical path.

concepts.label: Compute-optimal frontier
concepts.claim: Controlled sweeps fit a compute-optimal balance of about 20 tokens per parameter, so a run whose unique tokens per parameter sit well below it is data-starved and repeats its corpus, which is the regime where selection rather than more compute moves the run toward the frontier.

concepts.label: Selection engineering on the data path
concepts.claim: Selection removes accelerator work but adds host hashing, scoring passes, scattered reads, and shard coordination, so a retained subset saves reads only if materialized into its own shards, and data echoing recovers idle accelerator cycles when host preparation is the slow stage.

concepts.label: Static pruning with coverage floors
concepts.claim: Deduplication, quality pruning, and coreset selection shrink training work before training, but a score ranking must be constrained by per-class or per-slice coverage floors, which carry an explicit opportunity cost and can make a budget infeasible.

concepts.label: Dynamic selection
concepts.claim: Because sample value changes as the model learns, curriculum learning reorders data by difficulty and pacing, and active learning turns labeling into a query loop whose label saving must be measured against a budget-matched random baseline after pool-scoring cost.

concepts.label: Synthetic data as a lever
concepts.claim: When the pool lacks the needed cases, augmentation and generative synthesis replace curation at a per-sample cost against realism, the domain gap needs randomization, adaptation, and a real-data anchor, and recursive training risks model collapse.

concepts.label: Learning from unlabeled data
concepts.claim: Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning trade extra training compute for fewer task labels, valid only when the unlabeled pool matches the target distribution, and a foundation model pays off only when pretraining is amortized across enough downstream tasks.

concepts.label: Data cost and amortized ROI
concepts.claim: Total data cost is acquisition plus labeling plus storage plus processing, and a selection investment is judged by amortized return across all the runs it serves, so a pipeline that loses money on one run can pay across a campaign.

concepts.label: Accuracy-efficiency frontier
concepts.claim: Structure-preserving changes can move a dominated model toward the accuracy-efficiency frontier at little quality cost while structure-altering ones trade along it, so the engineer stops at an operating point that meets explicit quality and resource thresholds rather than at a visual knee.

concepts.label: Compression fits a deployment budget
concepts.claim: A deployment budget grants memory, time, and energy per result, and compression works three tiers (what the model computes, how many bits each value takes, how the result executes) after identifying the binding term, since a phone vision model spends its frame on arithmetic and LLM decode spends its token on weight bytes.

concepts.label: Structured vs unstructured pruning
concepts.claim: Pruning removes the weights or structures with the smallest loss impact, but only structured removal (channels, heads, layers, or 2:4 groups) yields smaller dense or hardware-supported tensors, and scattered zeros saved in a dense tensor save nothing.

concepts.label: Quantization regimes and the cliff
concepts.claim: Accuracy holds on a plateau down to some bit width and then falls off a model-dependent cliff, so post-training quantization over a calibration set comes first and quantization-aware training is spent only when it misses the quality target.

concepts.label: When fewer bits run faster
concepts.claim: Fewer bits speed a compute-bound layer only through a faster integer datapath but speed a bandwidth-bound decode in proportion to bytes removed, and only when dequantization is fused into the matmul, so the same precision change gives different gains in different regimes.

concepts.label: Combined techniques do not multiply
concepts.claim: Compression techniques interact through shared distributions, shapes, and kernels, so the default order is structure first, distillation as recovery, quantization last, with profiling after each step, and a 2x prune times a 4x INT8 gives an 8x ratio on paper but a fraction of that measured.

concepts.label: Measured deployment evidence
concepts.claim: Parameter, FLOP, and bit-width reductions are upper bounds, so a compressed artifact is accepted only on a measured profile on the target (accuracy, calibration, latency, throughput, size, energy), and model-only speedups are capped by the non-model share of end-to-end latency.

concepts.label: Affine quantization mechanics
concepts.claim: Quantization maps a clipping range onto integer levels with a scale and zero-point, range calibration trades clipping against resolution, per-channel scales beat per-tensor when ranges differ, and integer matmuls accumulate in INT32 and requantize.

concepts.label: Sparse storage break-even
concepts.claim: Unstructured sparsity pays only past a break-even, since an index beside each value doubles per-element bytes and irregular gathers keep sparse kernels slower than dense until high sparsity, whereas 2:4 structured sparsity halves the payload with fixed metadata.

concepts.label: Compression-specific fusion
concepts.claim: Some fusions exist only once a graph is compressed: batch normalization folds into the preceding convolution's weights and bias after structure stops changing, and weight-only kernels must dequantize in registers or a separate dequantize kernel restores the traffic quantization removed.

concepts.label: Knowledge distillation
concepts.claim: A compact dense student trained on a teacher's temperature-softened outputs moves cost from repeated inference to one extra training phase, runs on ordinary dense kernels, and is bounded by student capacity and teacher calibration.

concepts.label: Low-rank factorization
concepts.claim: Truncated SVD replaces a matrix with two thin factors, but the saving becomes speed only if the two factor kernels and the staged intermediate cost less than the original dense kernel.

concepts.label: Input-dependent computation and NAS
concepts.claim: Early exit, conditional layers, and mixture-of-experts spend less work on easy inputs but fragment batched execution and keep all experts resident, while hardware-aware architecture search is justified only by unusual targets or deployment scale (awareness).

concepts.label: Accelerator anatomy
concepts.claim: Every ML accelerator is matrix, vector, and special-function units beside on-chip memory, a wide off-chip path, and a host link, and it wins by spending on dense arithmetic and local storage the transistors a CPU spends on speculation and coherence, which pays only when the workload exposes the supported operation, precision, and parallelism.

concepts.label: Matching primitives to execution units
concepts.claim: Learned layers reduce to element-wise vector work, matrix multiply, and special functions, and each binds to the unit whose reuse matches it, so routing a primitive to the wrong unit collapses throughput to a fraction of peak.

concepts.label: Operand-supply hierarchy
concepts.claim: Delivered throughput is set by where operands live, with registers and SRAM supplying the array at its rate while HBM, host memory over PCIe, and flash fall off a bandwidth taper, so the diagnostic is traffic across each boundary, not capacity alone.

concepts.label: Energy ladder
concepts.claim: A DRAM access costs on the order of a hundred times an arithmetic operation or an on-chip SRAM read, so data movement, not arithmetic, is the primary energy target, and locality structures such as systolic arrays earn their area by avoiding the costliest event on the ladder.

concepts.label: Amdahl's law
concepts.claim: Acceleration speeds only the fraction p of baseline time on the accelerated path, so speedup is 1/((1-p) + p/A) and never exceeds 1/(1-p), and the unaccelerated fraction is defined by the intervention (data loading, host overhead, unsupported operators, launches).

concepts.label: Roofline and ridge point
concepts.claim: Attainable performance is the minimum of peak rate and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity, the ridge point (peak over bandwidth) marks where a kernel turns compute-bound, and intensity depends on implementation and batch, so the roofline bounds performance while profiling names the mechanism below the bound.

concepts.label: Stationary dataflows
concepts.claim: Every matmul operand is reused along a different loop and local storage can hold only one cheaply, so the loop order decides which operand stays (weight-, output-, or input-stationary) and two identical schedules can differ many-fold in traffic.

concepts.label: Tiling
concepts.claim: Tiling partitions an operation into blocks that fit a fast memory tier so each block is reused before eviction, with tile size bounded by every live buffer and dimensions off the tile grid paying a fringe penalty.

concepts.label: Compilers and runtimes
concepts.claim: ML compilers apply graph rewrites, kernel selection, memory planning by liveness, and scheduling over a mapping space too large for hand tuning, and runtimes dispatch precompiled tactics within declared shape ranges.

concepts.label: Heterogeneous SoCs and CMOS power
concepts.claim: Phone and embedded chips put CPU, GPU, DSP, and NPU on one shared memory system under a few-watt envelope managed by DVFS, where dynamic power scales roughly as frequency cubed, which is why accelerators favor wide arrays at moderate clocks.

concepts.label: Choosing an accelerator
concepts.claim: No datasheet chooses a machine because the binding resource belongs to the workload on that machine, so cost and energy are divided by throughput delivered on the binding resource, not by advertised peak.

concepts.label: Multi-chip scaling within a node
concepts.claim: Past one accelerator each added boundary lowers bandwidth and raises latency, so partitioning pays only when saved compute exceeds exposed communication (awareness in Vol I).

concepts.label: Reduced-precision and sparse datapaths
concepts.claim: Narrower formats help twice, fewer bytes per operand and more multiply-accumulate units per area, but only on a supported kernel with a wide accumulator, and 2:4 sparse units stream compressed weights plus position metadata for an advertised 2x.

concepts.label: Fusion limits on accelerators
concepts.claim: Fusion on an accelerator is limited by register pressure, occupancy, and reductions, so a fused kernel that holds intermediates on chip trades on-chip capacity for removed memory traffic.

concepts.label: Measurement validity
concepts.claim: Every speed, size, or energy number holds only for the conditions the measurement fixed (warm or cold, batch size, curated or deployed inputs, burst or sustained), so a benchmark is a proxy and the first question is what it does not measure.

concepts.label: Benchmark specification
concepts.claim: A claim becomes testable only when the benchmark fixes the input and output boundary, a quality floor, the model and runtime, the metrics, an open-loop synchronized harness, and recorded run rules, and a number reported without them cannot be reproduced or refuted.

concepts.label: Benchmark granularity
concepts.claim: Micro-benchmarks isolate kernels, macro-benchmarks expose composition across a model, and end-to-end benchmarks time the full request path, and a component speedup is diluted by every stage it does not touch.

concepts.label: Latency distribution and the SLO
concepts.claim: Mean latency hides the tail, so serving benchmarks report percentiles under a stated offered load and judge them against an SLO (a target for a named indicator, distinct from a contractual SLA), and generative workloads report time to first token and time per output token together.

concepts.label: Differences beyond noise
concepts.claim: Run-to-run variance and finite test sets give every measurement an uncertainty, so a comparison needs repeated, order-randomized runs with a stated interval and a prespecified minimum effect, accuracy comparisons need paired tests, and nonsignificance never establishes equivalence.

concepts.label: Quality beyond accuracy
concepts.claim: Compression and deployment can leave top-1 accuracy nearly unchanged while degrading calibration and accuracy on rare slices, so a model is accepted against absolute gates set in advance (aggregate accuracy, calibration error, deployment-critical slices).

concepts.label: Verification gap
concepts.claim: A finite evaluation certifies behavior only on the population it sampled and only within the uncertainty its sample size allows, because a test set covers an effectively zero fraction of the input space, so evaluation is statistical evidence and never proof.

concepts.label: Time to quality target
concepts.claim: A training benchmark scores wall-clock time until validation quality first reaches a fixed target, and scaling efficiency across accelerators reveals a loss without attributing it.

concepts.label: Energy measurement boundary
concepts.claim: Energy is integrated power over a matched window inside a stated boundary (chip, node, or facility through PUE), so efficiency belongs to one operating point and a duty-cycled device's idle floor can set battery life.

concepts.label: Standardized benchmark suites
concepts.claim: Comparable evidence needs a shared reference workload, quality target, and run rules, as in MLPerf's closed and open divisions and its arrival scenarios, which is why one accelerator reports very different Offline and Server throughput.

concepts.label: Data benchmarks
concepts.claim: A data benchmark fixes a deployment slice, a leakage-resistant holdout, coverage minimums, label-quality audits, and drift thresholds before aggregate scores mean anything, and saturated static benchmarks stop discriminating.

concepts.label: Throughput-latency measurement
concepts.claim: Throughput and latency are measured together because batching raises throughput while adding latency, so a throughput number without its latency percentile and offered load says nothing about a serving deadline.

concepts.label: Serving inverts training
concepts.claim: Once a model answers live requests the objective flips from long-run throughput to per-request latency at an SLO percentile, batch-one execution exposes weight traffic and launch overhead, and the machine target shifts from maximum utilization to headroom.

concepts.label: Latency budget
concepts.claim: End-to-end latency is a zero-sum budget spent serially on ingress, deserialization, preprocessing, transfer, queueing, inference, postprocessing, and egress and met at a stated quantile, so a faster model yields far less end-to-end gain when host stages dominate.

concepts.label: Queueing sets headroom
concepts.claim: Little's law sizes the in-flight population and the M/M/1 model shows time in system rising nonlinearly with utilization, so capacity is sized as the utilization a percentile SLO permits, and under overload only admission control or graceful degradation preserve latency.

concepts.label: Batching trades latency for throughput
concepts.claim: Batching amortizes fixed per-batch costs so saturated capacity grows almost linearly while fixed cost dominates, but every request pays formation delay, dynamic batching bounds it with a size-or-timeout trigger, and latency, memory, or the engine cap, not throughput, sets the largest useful batch.

concepts.label: LLM serving phases
concepts.claim: Token streaming splits latency into time to first token (prefill) and time per output token (decode), batching decode shares the weight stream but not cache reads, continuous batching reclaims slots as sequences end, and chunked prefill bounds the stall a long prompt imposes on active decodes.

concepts.label: KV cache budget bounds concurrency
concepts.claim: After weights, remaining device memory divided by per-conversation cache bytes sets how many conversations one accelerator holds, so context length and batch trade against each other, and paged allocation, prefix caching, and offloading change that budget.

concepts.label: Static vs dynamic inference
concepts.claim: Static (offline, batch) inference precomputes predictions into a store and runs throughput-first, while dynamic (online, real-time) inference evaluates inputs on demand inside the request path under the latency budget its SLO sets.

concepts.label: Cold start and model loading
concepts.claim: A new replica pays weight transfer, context creation, graph compilation, allocation, and warmup before its first useful request, so autoscaled capacity arrives late, and precompiled engines, memory-mapped formats, and warm pools shorten it.

concepts.label: Runtime and precision selection
concepts.claim: The deployment target narrows the runtime family and export coverage decides feasibility, and at batch one most of the speedup over eager execution comes from removing per-operation dispatch, while lower precision pays at large batch subject to calibration.

concepts.label: Host-path optimization
concepts.claim: Between socket and silicon a request crosses graph-to-kernel, host-to-accelerator, CPU, and storage boundaries, and timeline profiling locates which binds (idle bubbles, launch trains, synchronous copies, OS noise).

concepts.label: Serving economics
concepts.claim: Cost per inference is allocated hourly cost over completed inferences that meet the SLO, so the cheapest hardware at saturation wins only above a breakeven sustained load and capacity is sized from SLO-qualified throughput.

concepts.label: Speculative decoding
concepts.claim: A small draft model proposes several tokens that the target model verifies in one pass, yielding more than one token per target weight stream at batch one when the acceptance rate is high.

concepts.label: Operations loop
concepts.claim: Every production model runs detect, diagnose, decide, release, and recover, each step a control with a concrete machine cost, across three interfaces (data-model consistency, model-infrastructure parity, production feedback) where debt accumulates when a boundary erodes.

concepts.label: Layered monitoring and detection delay
concepts.claim: Silent failure is made visible only by layered monitoring (infrastructure telemetry, input checks, label-free drift statistics, outcome metrics joined to matured labels), and confirmation speed is bounded by labeled-outcome arrival, so drift signals must route to an owner with a deadline.

concepts.label: Safe release and tested rollback
concepts.claim: A validated checkpoint is not yet a safe release: exposure is staged (shadow, canary, blue-green), every node is verified to run the intended version, and rollback is tiered, tested, and state-aware, because cached state survives a weights-only revert.

concepts.label: Release safety costs resident memory
concepts.claim: Every shadow, canary, A/B arm, or standby keeps a second full model copy resident regardless of its traffic share, so release strategy is a memory decision for capacity-bound models and must be scheduled together with retraining on one node.

concepts.label: Request-keyed parity testing
concepts.claim: Training-serving skew is caught by replaying recorded inputs through the versioned training and serving transformations and comparing values per request ID, because marginal distribution screens can miss swapped values and flag real population shift.

concepts.label: Reproducibility and the model registry
concepts.claim: Exact replay requires freezing code, data, configuration, and environment plus deterministic kernels, content-addressed lineage traces an incident to its inputs, and a model registry holds immutable versions with lifecycle states so release machinery can promote or roll back the exact evaluated artifact.

concepts.label: Retraining economics
concepts.claim: Retrain only when expected recovered value exceeds compute, validation, deployment, and rollout-risk cost, and under locally exponential decay the cost-minimizing interval grows with the square root of run cost, so a fourfold change moves it only twofold.

concepts.label: Hidden technical debt
concepts.claim: ML debt compounds through statistical coupling that code review cannot see (entanglement, correction cascades, undeclared consumers, feedback loops, glue code), and each pattern names the infrastructure that pays it down.

concepts.label: A/B release decisions
concepts.claim: An A/B release decision needs a randomization unit, a power-derived sample size, guardrail metrics, and a preregistered horizon, and a non-significant result is inconclusive rather than a license to ship.

concepts.label: Incident response
concepts.claim: An ML incident is a statistical signal without a stack trace, so response classifies severity by impact, contains in parallel with diagnosis, debugs data-first, restores the whole contract rather than just the weights, and turns each incident into a new check.

concepts.label: Cost of observability
concepts.claim: Telemetry is an operating cost rate set by series, sample rate, ingest, and retention, so sampling, cardinality control, and tiered retention set the budget, and monitoring earns its keep only through harm it prevents.

concepts.label: Operational maturity
concepts.claim: A readiness score over data, model, infrastructure, and monitoring tests takes the minimum, so a perfectly validated model with no monitoring scores zero, and maturity is judged by which missing control to add next.

concepts.label: Proxy misalignment
concepts.claim: A model can pass verification while failing validation because harm enters through an incomplete specification: proxy features carry protected signal, proxy targets encode the inequity they measure, and an optimized proxy decouples from the goal while every health check stays green.

concepts.label: Fairness criteria as release gates
concepts.claim: Disaggregated evaluation turns fairness into a release gate with per-slice demographic parity, equal opportunity, or equalized odds, criteria that cannot all hold under unequal base rates, so the criterion is a justified policy choice and each slice test returns pass, fail, or insufficient evidence.

concepts.label: Fairness mitigation and its price
concepts.claim: A disparity is closed before training (reweighting), during training (adversarial debiasing), or after training (group thresholds), and each choice is a point on a fairness-accuracy frontier whose cost must be stated as a number.

concepts.label: Bias feedback loops
concepts.claim: When decisions censor future labels, disparity evolves geometrically across retraining intervals, so a gate passed at launch is a statement about the first interval, the feedback factor fitted from audits projects the breach, and randomized exploration is the serving cost that keeps it below one.

concepts.label: Lifecycle TCO
concepts.claim: A lifecycle total cost of ownership sums every training cycle, recurring inference, and operations, and for a high-traffic service the recurring inference term can exceed all training cycles many times over, so the dominant term is measured rather than assumed.

concepts.label: Energy to carbon
concepts.claim: Operational carbon is IT energy times PUE times grid carbon intensity, embodied carbon is a separate and sometimes majority term, and an optimization is responsible only if measured lifecycle energy and emissions fall for the same workload and quality target.

concepts.label: Specify before training
concepts.claim: Specification fixes the target, the named populations, and the human-oversight boundary before training forecloses them, and naming a subgroup fixes a per-group data budget, so stratified recruitment costs far less than random sampling for a rare group.

concepts.label: Explanation cost on the serving path
concepts.claim: An explainability requirement is an architecture choice, either an interpretable model that gives up capacity or a post-hoc attributor whose cost sits on the serving path and whose fidelity and stability must be measured.

concepts.label: Model cards and datasheets
concepts.claim: A model card records intended use, performance factors, and disaggregated metrics and a datasheet records the data's provenance and composition, together stating the envelope the model was validated in so that reuse outside it is detectable.

concepts.label: Privacy and governance as architecture
concepts.claim: Each regulatory obligation maps to a capability with a machine cost (staffed review, lineage-driven deletion, audit-log bytes), and differential privacy adds a second layer beyond access control at a measurable compute and memory price.

concepts.label: Federated learning
concepts.claim: Federated learning trains on clients that keep their raw data and send model updates to a coordinator, trading centralization risk for uplink traffic, client dropout, and divergent local updates, and it bounds what leaks only when combined with secure aggregation and differential privacy.
